anatomy.lede: Every part of a bottlenose dolphin is shaped for life in water: a smooth, torpedo-shaped body with no hair, no external ears and no hind limbs, steered by flippers and a tall fin.

hotspots.label: Beak (rostrum)
hotspots.text: Like all modern whales and dolphins, its skull is 'telescoped': the jaws are drawn out into a tapering beak and the nostrils have moved to the top of the head, so it can breathe while swimming.

hotspots.label: Toothed jaws
hotspots.text: The teeth grip slippery prey but do no chewing; fish are swallowed whole, head first.

hotspots.label: Flipper
hotspots.text: The front limbs are flippers, used with the dorsal fin and tail flukes for steering and swimming.

hotspots.label: Dorsal fin
hotspots.text: The dorsal fin is tall and curved and sits near the middle of the back.

hotspots.label: Streamlined body
hotspots.text: A fusiform, hairless body reduces turbulence, letting the dolphin cruise at speed. The back is dark to light grey and the belly white, sometimes faintly pink.

senses.lede: In water that is often murky or dark, the bottlenose dolphin lives in a world of sound, and it keeps in close physical contact with its companions.

senses.name: Echolocation
senses.text: It sends out high-frequency clicks and listens for the echoes to find prey, a sense humans lack entirely.

senses.name: Passive listening
senses.text: Dolphins also find prey simply by listening for the sounds fish make, without clicking, and use sound to communicate with their group.

senses.name: Touch
senses.text: Gentle body contact such as rubbing is a regular part of social life, alongside play and aggression.

body.lede: A warm-blooded, air-breathing mammal that lives its whole life at sea needs special plumbing for warmth, sleep and breath-holding.

systems.title: Keeping warm
systems.text: Blubber, a body large relative to its surface, and vascular shunts that cool chosen organs keep its temperature steady. Its metabolism rises if the water drops below about 13 °C or climbs above 28 °C.

systems.title: Half-asleep
systems.text: A dolphin must surface to breathe, so it rests one side of its brain at a time while slowing down, staying conscious enough to breathe and react.

systems.title: Holding its breath
systems.text: From thousands of tagged dives off Bermuda, researchers estimated that adults can stay down for about 9–11 minutes before needing extra recovery time near the surface.

genome.lede: The bottlenose dolphin has one of the best-studied genomes of any marine mammal, used in research on metabolism and ageing.

findings.title: Two parents, two genomes
findings.text: A 2019 assembly from a 36-year-old female improved on the earlier reference genome and was the first for the species to separate the copies inherited from each parent.

findings.title: Chromosome by chromosome
findings.text: The Vertebrate Genomes Project has since produced a chromosome-level assembly of about 2.38 billion base pairs.

findings.title: A conserved karyotype
findings.text: Bottlenose dolphins have 44 chromosomes, the same number as the related Burrunan dolphin and Risso's dolphin.

mind.lede: Experiments and decades of field study have made the bottlenose dolphin a standard example of animal intelligence.

studies.title: Recognising itself
studies.text: Two dolphins marked with ink went to a mirror and twisted to inspect the marks, evidence of mirror self-recognition.

studies.title: Names without voices
studies.text: Dolphins recognised synthetic versions of familiar signature whistles with every feature of the caller's voice removed, showing the whistle's shape alone carries identity.

studies.title: Twenty years of memory
studies.text: Playback of the whistles of former tank mates showed dolphins recognise companions they have not heard for at least 20 years.

studies.title: Hunting plans
studies.text: Wild dolphins herd fish into tight balls, take turns charging the school, and pin prey against sandbars and seawalls.

survival.lede: Safety for a bottlenose dolphin lies in its group.

tactics.title: Shifting groups
tactics.text: Dolphins live in fission–fusion societies: groups from a few animals to more than 100 split and re-form, and adult males often travel in strongly bonded pairs.

tactics.title: Shared babysitting
tactics.text: Females in a group help care for each other's calves and protect them from predators.

tactics.title: Helping the injured
tactics.text: Dolphins have been seen supporting injured companions at the surface and guarding them from threats.

threats.title: Fishing gear
threats.text: Bycatch and entanglement in gillnets, trawls, traps and recreational lines are major threats.

threats.title: Polluted coasts
threats.text: Harmful algal blooms, chemical contaminants such as PCBs and oil spills harm coastal dolphins.

threats.title: Boats and noise
threats.text: Vessel strikes, illegal feeding and harassment, and ocean noise also take a toll.

life.lede: A bottlenose dolphin grows up slowly, with one of the longest childhoods in the sea.

stages.name: Pregnancy
stages.text: A single calf is born after a year-long pregnancy, often in warmer months.

stages.name: Calf
stages.text: Newborns are 84–140 cm long and 14–20 kg. A calf swims in 'baby position' in its mother's slipstream, which makes nursing easier and reduces drag.

stages.name: Youngster
stages.text: Calves usually stay with their mothers for three to six years.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Females can mature before males. Mothers calve every three to six years, and females as old as 45 have given birth.
